title: Pavlov’s Original Data Require an Extinction Process Beyond Monotonic Trace Loss
content: The most famous dataset in behavioral science has never been fitted. Pavlov’s Conditioned Reflexes (1927) reports trial-level salivary measurements from named dogs, yet quantitative associative theory has been parameterized on animal data collected after 1960 while the founding tables are cited as illustrations. Here we transcribe every numerical value stated in the prose of Lecture IV, the extinction lecture, into a page-anchored dataset and compare two model classes on it: single-state erasure, in which nonreinforcement degrades the sole learned trace, and inhibitory write, in which the trace persists intact beneath an accumulating inhibitory state. Four structural signatures reported by Pavlov — invariable spontaneous recovery, dis-inhibition by alien stimuli, extinction beyond zero, and temporary versus permanent restoration — are each unattainable within the single-state class and natural under the inhibitory write, and the lecture’s one exactly anchored contrast identifies the inhibitory decay rate: recovery from 3 to 6 drops across 23 unreinforced minutes requires γ ≈ 0.024 min⁻¹. The founding data of conditioning establish that extinction engages a process beyond monotonic loss of the conditioned trace — the second state Pavlov argued for verbally — and bound its decay rate.
